title: Make bounded inferences
summary: Combine clues from a passage to reach a supported conclusion while preserving uncertainty, scope and alternative explanations.

sections.title: Move one careful step beyond the words
content: A stated fact appears directly in the passage. An inference is a conclusion that follows when you connect stated clues. A valid inference must stay close enough to the text that every important part can be defended.
Ask first: does the question request what the writer states, or what the evidence suggests? Retrieve exact evidence before drawing any conclusion.

sections.title: Use Claim, Clues and Limit
content: Claim: express the smallest conclusion that answers the question. Avoid adding a motive, cause or prediction unless the evidence supports it.
Clues: identify at least two relevant details and explain how they work together. One isolated word is rarely enough for a strong inference.
Limit: preserve the passage's scope and uncertainty. Words such as likely, suggests, may and cannot determine keep a conclusion proportional to the evidence.

sections.title: Separate association from cause
content: Example clues: a return station was moved nearer the bus exit, picture signs were added, and the container-return rate then rose. Supported inference: the combined changes likely made returns easier.
Unsupported claim: the picture signs caused the entire increase. The passage changed two things at the same time, so it cannot show which change produced the result or how much each contributed.
A result that follows a change is associated with it. Causation needs stronger evidence that rules out competing explanations.

sections.title: Build an inference bridge
content: Make a three-column note: clue one, clue two, and the conclusion they jointly support. Underline the exact words that connect each clue to the conclusion.

Run the removal test: if an important part of the answer has no matching clue, remove it. Run the strength test: if the evidence shows possibility or association, replace proves, always or caused with a more accurate expression.

sections.title: Compare the reach of each option
content: For each option, mark supported details, contradicted details and details that are simply absent. The best inference contains only supported details and answers the exact question.
Check population, place and time. Evidence from six stalls over four Fridays does not automatically describe every stall, every weekend or the whole market in the future.

sections.title: Diagnose an inference that reaches too far
content: Single-clue leap: I treated one detail as sufficient when the conclusion required a chain of evidence.
Outside assumption: I used what usually happens rather than what this passage supports.
Causal leap: I changed happened after or was associated with into caused.
Scope leap: I generalised from the observed group or period to everyone or all future situations. Name the error before revising the claim.

sections.title: The container return experiment
content: Answer six inference questions about an original five-paragraph market report. Each answer must connect textual clues and retain the report's limits. Feedback appears after the complete group.
